schools.summary: Gill supposes Benjamin stayed away either to screen the offenders, or from a careless security that their brethren would never go to war over it, or from sheer pride; he notes what the Levite leaves out of his account, forbearing to call the men of Gibeah the sons of Belial, and observes that he takes the cutting up of the body upon himself lest anyone suppose that outrage had been theirs too.

Henry observes that no common head summoned the meeting, the people coming by the consent of one common heart, and thinks Mizpeh was chosen to spare small Shiloh the trouble of so great an assembly; he regrets that a fair hearing might have prevented all the mischief that followed, and notes that though only the Levite's testimony is recorded, the plural in the original shows more than one witness was heard, as the law required.

Clarke thinks the Lord was consulted at Mizpeh as well as at Shiloh, citing the Maccabean record that in Maspha was the place where they prayed aforetime in Israel, though he grants that before the Lord may mean no more than meeting in God's name; he also draws from the word for the chief men, corner-stones, that the chiefs are the strength of the people as the corners are of the walls.

Keil and Delitzsch deny that the phrase unto the Lord proves any sanctuary at Mizpeh, and infer Benjamin's absence from the silence about their coming and from the later need to send men to them; they also point out that nobody at Gibeah had said they meant to kill the Levite, who draws that himself from what befell his wife. Ellicott identifies the site with the watch-tower the Crusaders called Mountjoie, gets from the muster of four hundred thousand the fact that the wars of Canaan had cost Israel a third of its strength, and says plainly that the Levite colours the whole story in the way most favourable to himself.

debates.question: Was Mizpeh a sanctuary, or only a meeting-place?

sides.position: no sanctuary and no ark — the phrase means only that the court was held in the sight of Jehovah
the Lord was consulted there, as the later record of prayer at Maspha suggests
there is no difficulty in supposing the ark and Urim were brought, since the chapter later carries them to Bethel

outliers.note: Alone among them treats the Levite as an interested witness, noting that circumstances have been omitted from the earlier account and that his testimony is shaped to his own advantage.

themes: tell us, how was this wickedness

8.pericope_label: The demand made of Benjamin, and refused

schools.summary: Gill reads the messengers' errand as an attempt to get the offenders delivered up and so prevent bloodshed on either side, and notes with the others that the word for the tribes of Benjamin means its ten families.

Henry calls the embassy the hinge of the tragedy, since had Benjamin come to Mizpeh there would have been nobody to deal with but the men of Gibeah; he insists the Israelites were discreet in their zeal and would not have fallen on a whole tribe unless that tribe made itself accessory after the fact, and offers two accounts of the refusal — either the tribe was more debauched than the rest, or, as Bishop Patrick suggested, it resented being reminded of its duty by brethren from whom it scorned to be taught.

Clarke gives the sense of the oath as satisfaction before any man goes home, and says nothing could have been fairer than the demand, since only the murderers were asked for, so that the refusal proves the tribe would have acted the same part had they been present.

Ellicott doubts the received rendering of the lot, which may mean casting the lot upon Gibeah to divide its territory rather than going up by lot, and compares the sentence of the Amphictyonic council against Crissa; he explains the refusal by the spirit of solidarity that has often made a Highland clan defend a guilty member, and compares the tribe's obstinacy to the courage in a bad cause of the Phocians. Keil and Delitzsch note that the narrative here runs ahead of itself, and that in refusing a just demand Benjamin took the side of the guilty.

debates.question: Why did Benjamin refuse to give up the offenders?

sides.position: clan solidarity and the peculiarly fierce character of the tribe
either general depravity, their lot being a rich land like Sodom’s, or resentment at the interference of their brethren
plain depravity — the refusal amounts to saying they would have done the same

themes: we will not go to our tents
deliver us the men, the children of Belial

14.pericope_label: The muster, and the seven hundred slingers

schools.summary: Gill rejects Ben Gersom's view that the slingers were the seven hundred men of Gibeah, since the text puts them among all the people and it is unlikely that every inhabitant of one town was left-handed; he notes the irony that a tribe named son of the right hand should have so many left-handed men, and that Josephus wrongly cuts the number to five hundred.

Clarke takes left-handed to mean ambidextrous, and stops at the phrase rendered not miss, which is literally not sin — the true import of the word, since to sin is to miss the mark, and men miss the mark of happiness by aiming at sensual gratifications; he gathers the ancient fame of the sling around the Balearic islanders, who would not let their children eat until they had struck the bread down from a pole, and repeats the report of Ovid and Seneca that the leaden ball melted in the air from its own speed.

Ellicott explains that Benjamin could live only in cities, the Jebusites still holding Jerusalem, takes twenty-six thousand for the true number against the lower figures of Josephus and the Greek, and suspects the text about the slingers, since it is hard that one small city should furnish the whole choice contingent and a curious coincidence that both figures are exactly seven hundred; he calls Bochart's explanation of the hair's breadth from archers shooting a helmet crest learning fantastically misapplied. Keil and Delitzsch think neither muster too large, since the whole congregation was in the field but for Jabesh-gilead.

debates.question: Are the seven hundred slingers the same as the seven hundred men of Gibeah?

sides.position: no — the text places them among all the people, and one town could hardly be left-handed to a man
the text itself is doubtful here, the coincidence of the two figures being suspicious

themes: twenty and six thousand that drew sword
sling stones at an hair breadth

18.pericope_label: The oracle at Bethel and the first defeat

schools.summary: Gill takes the enquiry to have been made at Shiloh, perhaps by a deputation sent thither.

Henry observes that they never asked whether to go up at all, the case being plain, but only who should go first, which he takes to mean who should command, since the prince of the leading tribe would be general of the whole; he finds a reason for the answer in Judah, from whom our Lord was to spring, and a warning in it too, since the first post was the most dangerous — who would strive for precedency that sees the peril of it? On the defeat he offers three answers at once, that God's judgments are a great deep, that the battle is not to the strong, and that God was correcting Israel for their own sins.
Clarke holds that a deputation was sent to Shiloh, where Phinehas was, and notices what the oracle did not say: the Lord said Judah, but he did not say that they should conquer.

Keil and Delitzsch answer that Shiloh lay too far from the seat of war, so the ark was brought to Bethel on Benjamin's northern border, a place already consecrated by God's appearances to Jacob; Ellicott insists the word means Bethel and not the house of God, sees no obstacle to the high priest carrying the ephod wherever it was wanted, and draws from the naming of a tribe that the Urim and Thummim were more than a pair of lots, since the question put to them did not admit a mere yes or no.

debates.question: Where was the oracle consulted, at Bethel or at Shiloh?

sides.position: at Bethel, the ark having been fetched there because Shiloh was too far from the war
at Shiloh, where Phinehas was, probably by a deputation sent thither

themes: which of us shall go up first

22.pericope_label: The second enquiry and the second defeat

schools.summary: Gill finds the flaw in their mourning rather than their tactics, since they lamented the defeat and the loss of so many lives but not their own sins, and least of all the idolatry they had been guilty of.

Clarke states the reason directly, that the Israelites did not seek the protection of God at all but trusted in the goodness of their cause and the multitude of their army, and were humbled to learn that the race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong.

Ellicott hears compunction in the way they name the enemy, Benjamin my brother, an uneasy sense that God might not approve a fratricidal war after all; he lays this defeat, like the first, to overweening confidence, reckons that the two together cost the eleven tribes thirteen thousand more men than the whole Benjamite army numbered, and can explain such a massacre only by supposing the slingers had some vantage-ground, setting beside it the field of Crecy. Keil and Delitzsch describe the rally in words borrowed from an older commentary, that the people drew up again in the same place seeking out of pure vainglory to wipe out the disgrace of their defeat, and hold that the fault lay never in the war itself, which the law required, but in the spirit it was waged in.

debates.question: Why was a righteous cause twice defeated?

sides.position: they trusted the goodness of their cause and their numbers instead of seeking God’s protection
they mourned their losses but never their own sins, least of all their idolatry

themes: they wept before the Lord until even

26.pericope_label: The fast at Bethel and the promise of victory

schools.summary: Gill explains that Phinehas standing before the ark is the posture of the priest enquiring by Urim and Thummim, and that his presence proves the affair much earlier than the days of Samson, or the man must have been three hundred years old; he reads the same verse as putting the scene at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood.

Henry names the two things Israel had leaned on and now lets go, the goodness of their cause and their numbers, and says that being sure their cause was good they had thought it needless to ask a blessing on it, perhaps concluding that God owed them his favour; he watches what the promise of victory did to them, since being sure of their strength before they had thought stratagem beneath them, and now they lay an ambush as their fathers had at Ai — the assurance made them not remiss but industrious.

Clarke regrets that had they humbled themselves and fasted and sacrificed at the first they had never been discomfited, notes that this is the earliest place in Scripture where fasting appears as a religious act, and adds that it is now little used, which he takes for a proof that self-denial is wearing out of fashion; he identifies Phinehas with the priest of Peor and dates the war shortly after Joshua's death.

Ellicott distinguishes the sacrifices, the burnt offering consumed entire and typifying absolute self-dedication, the peace offering chiefly thanksgiving, observes that the earlier enquiry was made of Elohim and this one of Jehovah, and marks this as the first answer to carry a promise, against which he sets Napoleon's remark that Providence usually favours the strongest battalion; Keil and Delitzsch take the note about the ark to mean it was at Bethel only for a time, fetched from Shiloh for this war.

outliers.note: Notices that the grandson of Aaron and the grandson of Moses are the chief figures of these two wild stories, the one discharging the supreme functions of the high priest while the other, sunk to a wandering Levite, serves a schismatic image for a paltry wage.

themes: they wept and fasted until even
the ark of the covenant was there

29.pericope_label: The ambush, the feigned flight, and the rout

schools.summary: Gill notes that though promised success they still thought proper to use means, and though their numbers were great they fell back on art, as Israel had at Ai, the ambush being set at night on Josephus' authority; he will not let the stratagem take the credit, since for all the art and the numbers and the valour the victory was the Lord's, Benjamin having never lost until that day.

Clarke gives two reasons for drawing the defenders out of the town, that the ambush was to fire the city as soon as it was empty and that the slingers had an advantage within the walls which they would lose in open country; he sets out the disposition as three divisions, one at Baal-tamar, one in ambush, and one skirmishing in front of Gibeah.

Ellicott calls the stratagem exceedingly simple and primitive, notes that it had already served against Ai and Shechem, presses the name Baal-tamar back to some famous and therefore solitary tree — the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel — and supposes the rout ran that far before the smoke-signal was seen; on the bare tract the ambush broke from he lists a proper name in the Greek, caves in the Syriac, and a reading one letter distant giving the west of Gibeah. Keil and Delitzsch translate Baal-tamar as palm-place, surviving near Gibeah in the days of Eusebius, and defend the summary against critics who called it spurious.

debates.question: Why does the account give the result before the details?

sides.position: a habit of Hebrew historical writing, which states the general result as early as it can — those who call the summary spurious have simply missed it
either compilation from several sources, one of them apparently a poem, or the sheer age of a style a Roman would have called inconditus

themes: liers in wait round about Gibeah
let us flee and draw them from the city
twenty and five thousand and an hundred

37.pericope_label: The smoke signal and the flight to the wilderness

schools.summary: Gill adds from the Jewish commentators that a time was fixed as well as a sign, the men in ambush to break out when the defenders had been drawn far enough from the city, and describes the fire they made in the empty town as so large that the pillar of flame and smoke could be seen a great way off.
Clarke states the plain point about the whole passage, that from this verse to the end of the chapter the operations already reported in general are given in detail.

Ellicott takes the words of the verse for the actual terms of the agreement, prefers column or beacon to flame, and rejects the variant reading that would make the signal a sword, since the flash of a blade could never be seen at that distance, though it would have matched the shield that flashed treasonably from Athens before Marathon; he notes that what the Benjamites saw is literally the whole of the city going up, and names the tract they fled into the wilderness of Bethaven, explaining that fugitives on that side of the country always made for the fords of Jordan. Keil and Delitzsch complete the turn, Benjamin looking back at the smoke and being terrified as Israel wheeled about.

themes: the flame of the city ascended up to heaven

43.pericope_label: The pursuit, the rock Rimmon, and the extermination

schools.summary: Gill has them surrounded on every side, the army posted in several places and the country people coming out against them, and cites Josephus for their being cooped up in a hollow of a valley with no way out; he and Ellicott both notice that the slain and the survivors together fall a thousand short of the tribe's muster, and conclude with Ben Gersom and Abarbinel that the thousand must have fallen in the two earlier battles.

Clarke observes what the six hundred came to mean, since by them alone the tribe was preserved from utter extermination, and will allow the massacre no good side at all: the crime of Gibeah was great, but there was no adequate cause for the relentless extermination of a whole tribe, and in this there was neither justice nor judgment — which he lays where the book itself lays it, that there was no king in Israel and no man with authority to repress the workings of the mob.

Ellicott admits defeat on the phrase describing the trampling, reporting a place-name in the Greek and Luther, in their rest in others, and the Vulgate's line that there was no repose for the dying; he identifies the rock Rimmon with a steep cone of white limestone still bearing the name, adds that the six hundred may have dwelt in it quite literally since the hill has four large caverns, and spells out what the closing verse means — the absolute extermination of a whole tribe, men, women and children, cities and cattle. Keil and Delitzsch count the slain in stages and place Rimmon fifteen Roman miles north of Jerusalem, surviving in the village of Rummon.

debates.question: Can the destruction of the tribe be defended at all?

sides.position: it has a good side and an evil one — the motive was an intense horror of moral pollution, the execution ruthless savagery
no — there was neither justice nor judgment in it, and no adequate cause for exterminating a whole tribe

themes: they gleaned of them in the highways
six hundred men abode four months
as well the men of every city as the beast
